title: Qui, que, où and time expressions

tips.title: Qui is followed by a verb, que by a subject
tips.body: Look at the word after the gap. A verb, as in *le prof qui explique*, means *qui*. A subject, as in *le prof que j'aime*, means *que*. The test works for people and for things. Two things can sit between *qui* and its verb: an object pronoun or *ne* (*le prof qui m'aide*, *qui ne vient pas*). And after *que* a long noun subject sometimes comes after the verb (*le film que regardent mes parents*).

tips.title: Venir de: just out of doing it
tips.body: *Je viens de manger* looks like *I come from eating*, and that is the way to remember it: you have just come out of doing it. So *venir de* in the present is the English *have just*.

tips.title: Le jour où, never le jour quand
tips.body: After a word for a time, such as *le jour*, *l'année* or *le moment*, French uses *où*. English says *the day when* or just *the day*. In reading, *où* after a time word means *when*, not *where*.

tips.title: Same subject before and after
tips.body: *Après avoir* and *avant de* borrow the subject of the main clause. Before you write *Après avoir mangé, …*, check that whoever comes after the comma is the one who ate.

tips.title: No -ing after avant de, après, sans or pour
tips.body: English puts *-ing* after *before*, *after* and *without*. French uses the infinitive, or *avoir* + participle after *après*: *avant de partir*, *après avoir fini*, *sans réviser*, and *pour réussir* for *in order to succeed*. The one French preposition that takes an *-ant* form is *en*: *en travaillant* (by working, while working).

why.matters: Short sentences are easy to write and hard to read for long, because every idea needs its own subject and verb. *Qui*, *que* and *où* let you add a detail to a noun without starting again, and *avant de*, *après avoir* and *venir de* put events in order inside one sentence. Reading texts use them constantly, so recognising them means following a sentence to its end instead of losing track in the middle. In writing, they are how a Higher answer explains and narrates rather than lists.

examples.title: Le jour où
examples.body: English speakers write *le jour quand* because *the day when* feels natural. French uses *où* after any word for a time: *le jour où je suis parti*, *l'année où j'ai eu seize ans*. Reading texts use it constantly, and a student who reads *où* as *where* gets lost in the middle of the sentence.

steps.title: Qui joins a sentence on to a noun
steps.body:
A **relative pronoun** lets you add a whole clause to a noun instead of starting a new sentence. *Qui* is the one on the grammar list for **both tiers** (spec page 156).

> *J'ai une prof. Elle explique très bien.* \
> → *J'ai une prof **qui** explique très bien.* — I have a teacher who explains very well.

*Qui* stands for the noun and is the **subject** of the verb that follows, so it is followed straight away by a verb. It means *who* for people and *which* or *that* for things:

> *C'est un métier **qui** paie bien.* — It is a job that pays well.

*Qui* **never** shortens to *qu'*, even before a vowel: *un ami **qui** aime le sport*.

The verb after *qui* agrees with the noun *qui* stands for: *les élèves **qui** travaillent*, *moi, **qui** suis* … That is why you check the noun before you write the ending.

rows: J'ai une prof. Elle explique bien.
J'ai une prof qui explique bien.
C'est un métier. Il paie bien.
C'est un métier qui paie bien.
J'ai un ami. Il aime le sport.
J'ai un ami qui aime le sport.

steps.title: Que when the noun is the object (Higher)
steps.body: *Que* is a **Higher tier** relative pronoun (spec page 156). Use it when the noun is the **object** of the next verb, so *que* is followed by a **subject and then a verb**: > *Le métier **que** je voudrais faire est vétérinaire.* — The job (that) I would like to do is vet. > *C'est la matière **que** je préfère.* — It is the subject (that) I prefer. English often leaves *that* out; French never leaves out *que*. Before a vowel, *que* becomes *qu'*: *le stage qu'il a fait*. **The test:** what comes straight after the gap? A **verb** means *qui*; a **subject** (*je, tu, il, mon frère*…) means *que*. > *Le prof **qui** m'aide* — *qui*, because *m'aide* is a verb (with its object pronoun). \ > *Le prof **que** j'aime* — *que*, because *j'* is a subject. In the perfect tense with *avoir*, the participle agrees with the noun that *que* stands for, because it is a direct object placed before the verb: *la lettre **que** j'ai **écrite***.

visuals.alt: A table showing that qui is followed by a verb and que by a subject and verb, with que shortening to qu apostrophe before a vowel

check.prompt: Which word fills the gap? *C'est la ville ___ je préfère.*
check.solution: ***Que***, because the gap is followed by a subject, *je*, and *la ville* is the object of *préfère*. *Qui* would need a verb straight after it, and *où* would need the town to be the place where something happens.

steps.title: Où for places and times (Higher)
steps.body:
*Où* is also a **Higher tier** relative pronoun. It joins a clause to a **place** or a **time**:

> *Le collège **où** je suis a mille élèves.* — The school where I am has a thousand pupils.
> *C'est la ville **où** je suis né.* — It is the town where I was born.
> *Le jour **où** j'ai eu mes résultats, j'étais nerveux.* — The day (when) I got my results, I was nervous.

That last one catches English speakers: after a word for **time** (*le jour, l'année, le moment*), French uses *où* where English says *when* or nothing at all. *Quand* is wrong there.

Do not confuse the relative *où* with the question word *où ?* (where?). And *ou* without an accent means *or*.

the day (when) I got my results

steps.title: Before and after: avant de and après avoir (Higher)
steps.body:
Two structures put actions in order inside one sentence. Both are **Higher tier** (spec page 167), and both need the **same subject** for the two actions.

**Avant de + infinitive** — before doing:

> ***Avant de** partir, je dis au revoir.* — Before leaving, I say goodbye.

**Après avoir + past participle** — after having done:

> ***Après avoir** fini mes examens, je vais voyager.* — After finishing my exams, I am going to travel.

Verbs that take *être* in the perfect use ***après être*** instead, and the participle agrees with the subject. This is correct French, but the specification's list names only *après avoir*:

> ***Après être** arrivée au collège, elle a cherché la salle.* — After arriving at school, she looked for the room.

English uses *-ing* after *before* and *after*. French never does: *avant de partant* and *après finissant* are both wrong. *Before* takes the **infinitive**; *after* takes ***avoir* or *être* plus the participle**.

On both tiers, *pour* and *sans* also take the infinitive: *pour réussir* (in order to succeed), *sans réviser* (without revising).

visuals.alt: A table of English before and after phrases with their French structures, avant de plus infinitive, après avoir or après être plus participle, and sans plus infinitive

steps.title: Just done and busy doing: venir de and être en train de (Higher)
steps.body:
Two more time structures are on the **Higher tier** list (spec page 158).

**Venir de + infinitive** means **to have just done** something. The present tense of *venir* gives the English perfect:

> *Je **viens de** finir mes devoirs.* — I have just finished my homework.
> *Mes parents **viennent de** rentrer.* — My parents have just come home.

It looks like *coming from*, but it is about time, not movement. Read it as *I am just out of finishing*.

**Être en train de + infinitive** means **to be busy doing** something, in the middle of it:

> *Je **suis en train de** réviser pour mes examens.* — I am busy revising for my exams.

French has no *-ing* tense, so the plain present *je révise* already means *I am revising*. *En train de* adds the idea that you are **in the middle of it right now**.

I am in the process of revising

steps.title: Joining short sentences into one
steps.body: A sentence built with these structures is longer, but it has to stay clear. Join **two sentences at a time**, and check the pronoun or the verb form each time.

steps.title: À toi : relier
steps.body:
Choose the structure for each one, then write it.

1. The subject that I prefer is history.
2. The town where I live is small.
3. After eating, we went out.
4. I have just received my results.

For 1, *I* is a subject after the gap, so *que*. For 2, *où* after a place. For 3, *manger* takes *avoir*. For 4, *venir de* in the present.

steps.title: Longer sentences that stay clear
steps.body: The longest writing task at Higher asks you to explain and narrate across timeframes (spec page 33). These structures let one sentence carry an order of events, a reason and a detail: > ***Après avoir passé** une semaine dans l'entreprise **où** travaille mon oncle, j'ai compris que c'était un métier **qui** me plairait, **mais** je **viens de** découvrir qu'il faut faire cinq ans d'études.* Three habits keep a sentence like that under control: - **One new structure per clause.** The sentence above has *après avoir*, then *où*, then *qui*, then *venir de*, each in its own clause. - **Check the subject of *avant de* and *après avoir*.** *Après avoir mangé, le bus est arrivé* says that the bus ate. Both actions need the same subject. - **Say it aloud.** If you need to breathe twice, split it into two sentences. Notice *où travaille mon oncle*: after *où* (and after *que*), French often puts a long noun subject **after** the verb. Recognise it in reading; you do not need to copy it.

visuals.alt: A table breaking one long sentence into its four structures and the job each one does

check.solution: *Après avoir mangé, le bus est arrivé* says that **the bus** ate, because the subject of the main clause is also the one who did the *après* action. In the others the same people do both actions.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- *Qui* (both tiers) is followed by a verb; it never shortens to *qu'*.
- *Que* (Higher) is followed by a subject and a verb; *qu'* before a vowel; never left out as English leaves out *that*.
- *Où* (Higher) after a place or a time: *le jour où*, never *le jour quand*.
- *Avant de* + infinitive and *après avoir* + participle (Higher); *après être* for verbs that take *être* is correct but goes beyond the list; same subject for both actions.
- *Venir de* + infinitive = have just done; *être en train de* = be busy doing (Higher).
- *Pour* and *sans* + infinitive on both tiers.

rows: que, où, avant de, après avoir, venir de, être en train de

questions.prompt:
Write about 80 words in French about a week of work experience, real or imagined. Mention:

- where you did it and what the place was like
- what you did on the first day
- the best part of the week
- what you would like to do in the future

Use *qui*, *que* or *où*, and *avant de* or *après avoir*.
questions.solution:
**Modèle.**

> *J'ai fait mon stage dans une école primaire **où** travaille ma tante. C'était une école **qui** avait une grande bibliothèque. Le premier jour, **après avoir rencontré** les profs, j'ai aidé des enfants de six ans à lire. Ce **que** j'ai préféré, c'était le dernier jour, quand les enfants m'ont donné une carte. **Avant de partir**, j'ai dit merci à tout le monde. Plus tard, je voudrais devenir professeur, parce que c'est un métier **qui** change des vies.*

**What earns the marks.** *Où* after a place, *qui* twice as a subject, and *que* after *ce*. *Après avoir rencontré* and *avant de partir* both have *je* as their subject, like the main verbs. The past is told in the perfect and the imperfect, and the future in the conditional *je voudrais*. *Ce que*, *what*, is not on the grammar list, so you will not be tested on it; use it only if you are sure of it.

two or more relative pronouns correct
avant de or après avoir correct with the same subject

criteria.text: Covers all four points with some detail
Uses at least two relative pronouns correctly (qui, que, où)

Uses present, past and future or conditional timeframes

questions.prompt:
Translate into French:

1. I have a friend who lives in Paris.
2. The film that we saw was funny.
3. It is the town where I was born.
4. Before leaving, I phoned my mother.
5. I have just finished my exams.
questions.solution:
**Modèle.**

1. *J'ai un ami qui habite à Paris.*
2. *Le film que nous avons vu était drôle.*
3. *C'est la ville où je suis né.* (*née* for a girl)
4. *Avant de partir, j'ai téléphoné à ma mère.*
5. *Je viens de finir mes examens.*

**What earns the marks.** In sentence 1 *qui* is followed by the verb *habite*; in sentence 2 *que* is followed by the subject *nous*, and French cannot leave it out. Sentence 3 uses *où* after a place, and *naître* takes *être*. Sentence 4 uses *avant de* + infinitive where English has *-ing*, and *téléphoner à* needs its *à*. Sentence 5 uses the present of *venir de* for *have just*.

criteria.text: Sentences 1 and 2 with qui before a verb and que before a subject
Sentence 3 with où after a place and a correct perfect of naître
Sentences 4 and 5 with avant de + infinitive and venir de + infinitive

questions.modelAnswer:
**Modèle.**

1. *J'ai un ami qui habite à Paris.*
2. *Le film que nous avons vu était drôle.*
3. *C'est la ville où je suis né.* (*née* for a girl)
4. *Avant de partir, j'ai téléphoné à ma mère.*
5. *Je viens de finir mes examens.*

**What earns the marks.** In sentence 1 *qui* is followed by the verb *habite*; in sentence 2 *que* is followed by the subject *nous*, and French cannot leave it out. Sentence 3 uses *où* after a place, and *naître* takes *être*. Sentence 4 uses *avant de* + infinitive where English has *-ing*, and *téléphoner à* needs its *à*. Sentence 5 uses the present of *venir de* for *have just*.

questions.prompt: Which word fills the gap? *C'est la robe que j'ai ___ hier.*
questions.solution: ***Achetée.*** *Que* stands for *la robe*, a feminine singular direct object placed before *avoir*, so the participle agrees with it: *achetée*. Plain *acheté* ignores the agreement, and the plural endings would need more than one dress.

examTechnique.body:
In **reading and listening**, a relative pronoun means the sentence is not finished: keep going until you find the main verb. *Où* after a time word means *when*. *Venir de* means *have just* and *en train de* means *busy doing*; neither is about movement or trains.

In **translation into English**, you may drop the *that* French always writes (*le film que j'ai vu* is *the film I saw*), and turn *avant de* + infinitive into *before* + *-ing*.

In **writing and translation into French**, test every gap: a verb next means *qui*, a subject next means *que*. Check that the subject of *avant de* or *après avoir* is the subject of the main verb. At Higher tier, two or three of these structures in the long answer show that you can build a complex sentence.
examinerErrors: Leaving out *que* where English drops *that*: *le film nous avons vu*.
Writing *le jour quand* instead of *le jour où*.
Using *-ant* after a preposition: *avant de partant*, *après finissant*.
Writing *après avoir* with a verb that takes *être*: *après avoir sorti*.
A different subject after *après avoir*: *après avoir mangé, le bus est arrivé*.
Reading *je viens de* as movement: *I am coming from*.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer builds sentences of two or three clauses that stay clear: a relative clause adds a detail, *après avoir* or *avant de* puts two actions in order, and *venir de* marks something that has just happened. Every *qui* and *que* passes the verb-or-subject test, *où* follows a time as well as a place, and the subject of every *après avoir* is the subject of its main verb. In reading, it follows a long sentence through a relative clause to its main verb without losing track.
